docs.title: IRoC-U Technical Survival Guide: The Unfiltered Senior Handover
docs.text: "Look, if you're setting out to build a GPS-denied drone welcome to hell. But you're not alone. We burned cash, fried Flight Controllers, smoked Raspberry Pis, and lost countless nights of sleep so you don't have to repeat our dumb mistakes. Make good use of it."

docs.title: The Mindset: Don't Be A Hero, Iterate
docs.text:
The number one mistake you guys are going to make: "Bro, we'll straight up build a fully autonomous drone, we already wrote the ROS 2 nodes." Bullshit. If you jump straight into autonomous flight, you will turn \$500 worth of hardware into scrap metal on day one.

Follow this exact sequence. No shortcuts: 1. Fly Manually First: At least one person on the team needs to know how to fly comfortably in manual mode (Stabilize). If you can't even fly it by hand, what the hell makes you think your code will fly it autonomously? Make onep erson udnerstand all the modes and how does they work of the stack you using ; 2. Get Your Simulation Right: Everything must work flawlessly in SITL and Gazebo first. If your drone won't fly in sim, taking it to real hardware is an absolute crime. 3. Fight Sim2Real: Simulation is an ideal wonderland. Real hardware brings ground effect, air drag, motor vibrations, voltage drops, and dirty sensor noise. Sim2Real is a whole different beast. 4. Verify One Task At A Time: First stable hover -> then manual guided square -> then optical flow hold -> then visual odometry -> then autonomous waypoints. Test one single thing at a time. Whatevr maybe the task ; one task at a time ;

docs.title: The Golden Rules (Swear By These)
docs.text:
1. RECORD EVERY FUCKING THING: Every single flight test, every time you plug in a LiPo battery, after every crash, and after every tragedy—pull out your phone and record videos and photos. When hardware crashes or flips on takeoff, high-speed slow-mo video is the only thing that will tell you whether a prop shattered first or the autopilot disarmed.
  2. Get Yourself 2 Mechanical Guys (PLEASE): Computer engineering students always assume software can fix everything. When motor shafts don't fit your props, frame vibrations make the EKF freak out, and your 3D mounts snap like twigs, you will sit in the lab and cry. Keep two dedicated mechanical teammates to handle structural rigidity, motor mounts, and prop tolerances.
  3. Embrace AI Tools (Claude Code / Codex): I was honestly a non-AI person before this, and I realized my mistake way too late. Competitions run on a completely different speed and mindset. Get Claude Code or Codex—they are ridiculously good. Even the core ArduPilot and PX4 dev communities are heavily embracing AI tooling now. Use AI to scaffold boilerplate and debug nasty ROS 2 setups, but keep your brain turned on.
  4. The Discord Community Is Your Lifeline: When you're stuck, don't bang your head against the wall for 10 hours. Hop onto the ArduPilot Discord; the core devs there are insanely helpful:
  5. @RyanF (The god of DDS / Micro-ROS)
  6. @RhysMainwaring (Gazebo simulation and GROS)
  7. @PeterBarker (General dev, core ArduPilot & SITL)
  8. @NateMailhot (General dev & EKF wizard)
  9. @AndyPiper (General dev & modern tooling)

docs.title: Survival Guide Index
docs.text:
The entire guide is split across these 6 modules. Go through them step-by-step:

  1. 01 - SITL and Gazebo SITL + Gazebo setup, joystick RC hacks, gimbal panics, the GStreamer trap, and custom 3D worlds.
  2. 02 - ROS 2 vs PyMAVLink & DDS PyMAVLink vs ROS 2, MAVROS vs DDS (the 1MB FC RAM limit trap), GCS picks, and hacking custom firmware binaries.
  3. 03 - Optical Flow and Rangefinder First steps in GPS-denied: replicating MTF-01 optical flow + rangefinder, tweaking EKF parameters, and why custom precision landing scripts are a waste of time.
  4. 04 - ORB-SLAM3 and ROS 2 TF ORB-SLAM3 on Ubuntu 24.04 (hunting community forks), RealSense depth feeds, /ap/tf, tracking states, and the FRD vs FLU coordinate frame nightmare.
  5. 05 - Hardware Fails & Reality Checks Smoke stoppers, frying Pis via GPIO, brownouts, short motor shafts & 1045 self-locking props, the 3 CCW + 1 CW blunder, and our honest benchmarking disaster.
  6. 06 - Reading Dataflash Logs & Debugging Learning to read Dataflash .bin logs, catching EKF innovation blowups, vibration clipping, and injecting custom debug prints directly into ArduPilot source code.

Good luck. Break less hardware, fly more.

docs.title: Title: Simulation First - SITL, Gazebo, and Day One Headaches
docs.text:
The Concept: Setting up SITL (Software In The Loop) paired with the Gazebo simulator is your absolute first line of defense. Before you even dare to touch physical hardware, you have to test your flight dynamics, gimbal movements, camera feeds, and autonomous commands inside a simulated physics environment without blowing a hole in your wallet.

How Should You Try : - You can fly drone without hardware ; get the basics right ; instead of RC Transmitor use Joystick. - The camera gimbal on the Iris drone refused to tilt down in Gazebo, should foolow how to add sitl peripherals ig . - Build opencv with gstreamer if not using ROS. - you need to learn early on how to import custom 3D environments from Blender (like Mars terrain or indoor obstacle courses) into Gazebo.

The Jargon: - SITL (Software In The Loop): Running the actual ArduPilot autopilot firmware on your PC as a standalone C++ process without needing any physical flight controller board. - Gazebo (Garden/Harmonic): A 3D physics simulator that accurately mimics gravity, aerodynamics, contact forces, and virtual camera/gimbal sensor plugins. - MAVProxy: A lightweight command-line Ground Control Station that connects to your SITL instance by default and lets you dynamically load autopilot modules. - GStreamer: A multimedia pipeline framework used to stream live video feeds from Gazebo virtual cameras to Python or OpenCV scripts with minimal latency.

The Task (Do It Yourself): - Step 1: Follow the official ArduPilot documentation to install SITL and Gazebo on your operating system, and successfully spawn an Iris quadcopter. - Step 2: Plug in a joystick or gamepad, configure your axis mapping, and execute the basic takeoff sequence: ARM -> FLIGHTMODE (GUIDED) -> TAKEOFF. - Step 3: Run module load gimbal in MAVProxy to unlock gimbal tilt control, grab the live camera stream from Gazebo, and write a simple script to run a basic color detection algorithm (e.g., tracking a bright red or blue marker). - Step 4: Swap out the default runway world: grab a 3D surface mesh from Blender or download a Mars terrain environment, and load the Iris quadcopter inside it. - Question for you: If your drone says "ARMED" in the console and your motors are audibly spinning in Gazebo, but the drone sits glued to the floor and won't lift off, did you forget your EKF origin/GPS lock, or is your motor thrust scaling messed up?

Where to find the answers: - ArduPilot Official Gazebo Guide: ArduPilot with Gazebo - MAVProxy Modules Documentation: MAVProxy Gimbal Module Documentation - Community Support: Check out the relevant channel on the ArduPilot Discord and ping @RhysMainwaring.

docs.title: Title: Software Architecture - ROS 2 vs PyMAVLink, DDS, and GCS Chaos
docs.text:
The Concept: You have two primary routes to get your companion computer talking to your Flight Controller (FC): the lightweight PyMAVLink path (sending raw MAVLink packets) or the modern full-blown robotics stack with ROS 2 (using the native DDS Micro-ROS bridge or legacy MAVROS). Picking the right setup comes down to your FC's available RAM and how much overhead your autonomy stack can tolerate.

Keep things in Mind: - The DDS vs MAVROS trap: To run DDS, your FC needs more than 1MB of RAM/Flash (like STM32H7 chips). If your FC has under 1MB of RAM, the DDS binary isnt recommended by @Ryanf . - Getting overwhelmed by Ground Stations: On Linux, everything technically runs—Mission Planner (running through the Mono runtime), QGroundControl (QGC), MAVProxy, and for quick browser-based setup, mico config (an online configurator) felt pretty convenient too.Make a simple rule early: use MAVProxy in SITL for fast scripting and terminal checks, but once you're tuning real hardware on the field, stick to Mission Planner for rock-solid telemetry and parameter handling. - Flying completely blind on coordinates: When we sent position coordinate commands from our companion computer, we had zero clue what numbers were actually reaching the FC. I realized way too late that you can jump right into ArduPilot's source code, drop custom debug print statements, compile a custom binary, and flash it to watch the raw coordinates land live inside your GCS! For fuck sake do this early on;

The Jargon: - MAVLink: A lightweight binary telemetry protocol that ArduPilot speaks natively. - PyMAVLink: A Python wrapper library used to create and parse MAVLink messages directly (the lightweight alternative to MAVSDK and the deprecated DroneKit). - MAVROS: A heavy ROS 1/2 node that acts as a translator, turning ROS topics into MAVLink packets over a serial or UDP port. - DDS (Micro-ROS Bridge): Data Distribution Service middleware where ArduPilot natively publishes and subscribes to ROS 2 topics (/ap/...) with no translation node in between (strictly requires >1MB RAM FC like Pixhawk 6C/6X). - GCS (Ground Control Station): Software (Mission Planner, QGC, MAVProxy) used to monitor drone telemetry, adjust parameters, and trigger flight modes.

The Task (Do It Yourself): - Step 1: Fly a basic autonomous navigation pattern in GUIDED mode: arm, take off, and fly a clean 5x5 meter square (first manually by typing coordinate commands into the MAVProxy terminal, then by writing an automated PyMAVLink script). - Step 2: Clone the ArduPilot repository, navigate to libraries/AP_DDS/, and inject custom debug console messages (gcs().send_text()) into the incoming external navigation topic handlers. - Step 3: Compile your custom binary (./waf configure --board sitl and ./waf copter), launch SITL, and verify that the companion computer's raw coordinates are printing out live on your GCS console. - Question for you: If you're stuck with a budget flight controller running an STM32F4 processor with low RAM, can you use the native DDS Micro-ROS architecture, or are you forced to fall back on MAVROS or PyMAVLink?

Where to find the answers: - ArduPilot DDS Official Guide: ROS 2 with ArduPilot DDS - PyMAVLink Documentation: PyMAVLink GitHub & Docs - Code Location: libraries/AP_DDS/ in the ArduPilot root directory. - Discord Mentors: Hit up @RyanF on the ArduPilot Discord (#ros).

docs.title: Title: GPS-Denied Transition - Optical Flow, Rangefinders, and EKF Drama
docs.text:
The Concept: In a GPS-denied arena, your autopilot doesn't have satellite fixes to fall back on. The Flight Controller desperately needs alternative sensors to calculate its position and velocity. An Optical Flow sensor tracks ground pixel shifts to estimate horizontal velocity, while a Rangefinder (Lidar/Sonar) measures altitude, fusing together inside EKF3 to give you a drift-free hover.

How Should you DO: - Don't Blindly trust the IMU: We naively assumed that the IMU (accelerometer + gyro) could handle dead reckoning and let us fly in GPS-denied spaces. It completely failed! IMU double-integration drift is so bad that the drone won't even arm in position-dependent modes (like LOITER or GUIDED). You need another source ; use MTF 01 module (rec). - Understand parameters: You have to tweak values yourself, and see what breaks and why. Try to make the necessary changes for GPS Denied - Replicate the Hardware you have in SITL : We tried adding an optical flow + rangefinder combo in SITL (trying to replicate an MTF-01 module) using SITL peripheral docs;

  • Wasting time on custom Precision Landing: I tried being heroes and wrote our own precision landing PID algorithm from scratch, thinking it would give us more granular control. It was a complete waste of time! ArduPilot's native Precision Landing mode is already rock solid and heavily battle-tested. Never reinvent the wheel when the built-in mode already works reliably.

The Jargon: - Optical Flow: A downward-facing camera sensor that tracks ground feature displacement to calculate the drone's horizontal velocity $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$. - Rangefinder (ToF / Lidar): A distance sensor measuring height above the ground; without it, optical flow cannot convert pixel movement into metric speed. - MTF-01: Microlink's popular integrated Optical Flow + Lidar module commonly used for GPS-denied indoor drone navigation. - EKF3 (Extended Kalman Filter 3): ArduPilot's multi-sensor fusion math engine that blends noisy IMU, optical flow, and rangefinder data into a stable position estimate. - Precision Land: A native ArduPilot flight mode that locks onto visual targets or beacons to land autonomously with centimeter-level accuracy.

The Task (Do It Yourself): - Step 1: Configure optical flow and rangefinder peripherals in SITL and set your EKF parameters (EK3_SRC1_POSXY = 0, EK3_SRC1_VELXY = 5 [OpticalFlow], EK3_SRC1_POSZ = 2 [RangeFinder]). - Step 2: Arm the drone in GPS-denied conditions inside LOITER mode and verify that it holds a stable hover without requiring manual stick corrections. - Step 3: Skip writing custom landing logic and configure ArduPilot's native Precision Landing mode to touch down on a designated target pad. - Question for you: If your rangefinder suddenly spikes to 0 or reads out-of-range (say, over a shiny or reflective floor), can EKF3 still trust your optical flow velocity data, and what happens to your altitude hold?

Where to find the answers: - ArduPilot Non-GPS Navigation: ArduPilot Non-GPS Navigation Hub - Optical Flow Sensor Setup: Optical Flow Configuration - Precision Landing Documentation: Precision Landing Docs - SITL peripherals , Add sensors to drone: SITL peripherals

docs.title: Title: Visual SLAM & Frames - ORB-SLAM3, ROS 2 TF, and Coordinate Hell
docs.text:
The Concept: Optical flow only works across flat surfaces for 2D velocity; true 3D spatial navigation in complex GPS-denied arenas requires Visual SLAM (like ORB-SLAM3). A depth camera (like an Intel RealSense RGB-D) computes a 3D pose estimate that your companion computer feeds into ArduPilot's EKF3 over the ROS 2 topic /ap/tf as external visual odometry.

How You SHould Proceed: - The Ubuntu 24.04 (Noble) build mismatch: The official ORB-SLAM3 repo does not build out-of-the-box on Ubuntu 24.04! C++ standards, Pangolin, and OpenCV versions are completely broken. We had to dig through community forks—one developer had forked ORB-SLAM3 core for 24.04, and someone else had created a separate fork for the ROS 2 wrapper! If a repo won't compile on your OS, don't give up: dive into GitHub issues and PRs, and grab a working community fork. - Ignoring camera calibration & intrinsics: If you have an Intel RealSense depth camera, you get factory-calibrated intrinsics out of the box. But if you use any other camera, you must print a checkerboard pattern and calibrate the lens to extract the intrinsic matrix. If you skip this, your SLAM will lose tracking every 5 seconds. - Ignoring Tracking States: We didn't bother reading the ORB-SLAM3 docs properly. We were blindly feeding coordinates to the FC without checking whether the tracking state was OK, RECENTLY_LOST, or completely LOST. When SLAM loses tracking and you feed old or garbage coordinates to the FC, the drone twitches violently and crashes. - Frame calibration and the FRD vs FLU nightmare: Our biggest disaster was coordinate frames. ROS 2 defaults to the FLU (Forward-Left-Up) frame, but ArduPilot's FC strictly expects coordinates in FRD (Forward-Right-Down: forward = +X, right = +Y, down = +Z). We wasted hours trying random time delays and axis flips based on blind guesswork. The real fix was diving into ArduPilot's libraries/AP_DDS/ (external_nav) source, adding coordinate print logs, and watching what numbers actually hit the FC. - Note on alternatives: ORB-SLAM3 isn't the only game in town. Many teams use OpenVINS or other visual odometry packages, and those work great too.

The Jargon: - ORB-SLAM3: A real-time visual SLAM library that tracks visual features to calculate a camera's 6-DoF trajectory and map its environment. - TF / TF2: ROS 2's coordinate transform library that keeps track of spatial relationships between sensor frames (camera_link, base_link, odom, map). - FRD vs FLU: Forward-Right-Down (standard aeronautical body frame used by ArduPilot) vs Forward-Left-Up (standard robotics body frame used by ROS). - Tracking State: ORB-SLAM3's internal health status (SYSTEM_NOT_READY, NOT_INITIALIZED, OK, RECENTLY_LOST, LOST). - Visual Odometry (VO): Estimating the drone's position and orientation changes by tracking feature movements across camera frames.

The Task (Do It Yourself): - Step 1: Attach an RGB-D / RealSense camera model to the Iris gimbal inside your Gazebo simulation, and verify that the /camera/depth and /camera/color image topics are publishing by changing gazebo models in ardupilot_gz_bringup package. - Step 2: Build ORB-SLAM3 core and its ROS 2 wrapper (using working community forks on Ubuntu 24.04), and publish the estimated camera pose to the /ap/tf topic. - Step 3: Go into libraries/AP_DDS/ in the ArduPilot repository, add debug print statements inside the external navigation handler, and verify that flying forward registers as +X, flying right registers as +Y, and moving downward registers as +Z inside the FC. - Question for you: If your camera's optical frame (+Z forward, +X right, +Y down) is fed directly into ArduPilot's FRD frame without applying a rotation transform, what will happen when you command the drone to hold altitude?

Where to find the answers: - ArduPilot Source: libraries/AP_DDS/ (specifically ap_dds/external_nav) in the ArduPilot repository. - External Navigation Docs: Vision-Positioning with ROS / DDS - ORB-SLAM3 Documentation: Official ORB-SLAM3 guides covering tracking states and camera models. - Adding Cameras : Depth Camera Ardupilot Disucssio Forum - Discord Mentors: Ping @RyanF on the ArduPilot Discord (#ros).

docs.title: Title: Hardware Fails - Smoke, Brownouts, and Ground Reality
docs.text:
The Concept: Everything looks clean and effortless in simulation, but physical hardware is governed by brutal real-world constraints. Clean power distribution, motor shaft mechanics, electrical protection, and proper companion computer power budgeting are the only things standing between a flight-ready drone and an expensive pile of charred ashes on your lab bench.

How We Messed Up: - NO SMOKE STOPPER, FRIED OUR FC: The very second we plugged in our LiPo battery, thick white smoke poured out of the Flight Controller! Whether it was a short circuit or reverse polarity, we had no idea because the board was already destroyed. If we had spent ten bucks on a smoke stopper, the circuit would have tripped and saved our FC. Make this rule number one: never connect a battery to freshly soldered hardware without a smoke stopper. - Powering the Pi through GPIO (Fried it): Raspberry Pi GPIO header pins have zero reverse-polarity or over-voltage protection. We fed 5V directly into a GPIO pin, and the Pi fried on the spot! Never power your companion computer through GPIO; always use a dedicated high-current UBEC. And if you're using a Raspberry Pi 5, there are specific config commands you need to run to handle USB power negotiation (usb_max_current_enable=1) so it runs at full throttle without throttling your peripherals. - Companion Computer Brownouts: Every time we tried to take off, our companion computer randomly shut down and rebooted! We were using a cheap, thin USB power cable that couldn't handle the current draw. When the motors throttled up, the main bus voltage dipped, and the board browned out. Use thick, high-gauge wiring and do proper power budgeting. - Cheap Depth Camera Cables: We tried running our RealSense depth camera using a generic cheap USB cable, which resulted in constant disconnects, dropped frames, and system crashes. Depth cameras strictly require expensive, high-grade, shielded USB 3.0 cables. - Cheap Plastic Frames vs Real Carbon Fiber: We bought cheap knock-off frames that looked like carbon fiber but shattered on our very first minor crash. Invest in real, rigid carbon fiber frames. Also, 3D print 2 or 3 spare copies of every single mount, bracket, and landing leg in advance so a broken piece doesn't kill your entire testing day. - Short Motor Shafts and 1045 Props: We ordered Holybro 2216 motors, but their shafts were too short for standard prop nuts. Regular props wouldn't fit or clamp down securely! For short-shaft motors like that, you need DJI-style self-locking props. - The 3 CCW + 1 CW Blunder: Due to some complication we ended up with three Counter-Clockwise (CCW) motors and only one Clockwise (CW) motor. A quadcopter literally cannot fly like that. Always make sure you have two matched CW and CCW pairs. (Its very hard for mechanically configured CW motor to use it as CCW mtoors) - Takeoff Disasters: Our drone flipped violently the moment we took off because our prop rotation directions were backward. 

On another test, it drifted aggressively sideways on liftoff because the RC sticks weren't calibrated.

If drone doesnt behave well on takeoff in any mode first check with those two issues and then check with esc replacement

  • Blindly Swapping ESCs: We looked at low frame rate video from a phone and decided an ESC was dead, buying a replacement without diagnosing the problem. Always stick to the sequence: RC Calibration -> Motor rotation check -> ESC calibration -> only replace the ESC if it still fails.

  • Benchmarking Failure : We never did proper performance benchmarking. We blindly guessed on vibes and gut feeling, and bought the wrong companion board! We didn't know whether our tasks needed a 16GB Raspberry Pi or a Jetson Orin Nano. Don't make our mistake: run your ROS 2 nodes and SLAM on your laptop first, profile the exact CPU and RAM loads, learn proper benchmarking methods, and buy the right companion computer based on data.

  • Soldering and Mechanical Teammates: Clean up your soldering technique early, keep connections modular, and keep an organized tackle box with spare JST-to-DuPont wires, extra screw kits, and zip bags. Find repair shops near you for expensive gear. And seriously: recruit two mechanical engineering teammates.

The Jargon: - Smoke Stopper: A resettable electronic fuse placed between the battery and the drone that instantly cuts power if it detects a short circuit. - UBEC (Universal Battery Elimination Circuit): A dedicated DC-DC step-down buck regulator that converts high battery voltage (14.8V - 25.2V) into a clean, regulated 5V DC high-amp output. - Brownout: A sudden microprocessor reset caused by a temporary voltage dip during high motor current draws. - Self-Locking Props: Threaded propellers that naturally tighten themselves in the opposite direction of motor rotation (mandatory for short-shaft motors). - ESC Calibration: Teaching your Electronic Speed Controllers the exact minimum (1000us) and maximum (2000us) PWM throttle endpoints from your autopilot.

The Task (Do It Yourself): - Step 1: Create a full Power Budgeting spreadsheet: peak motor current draw + ESCs + Flight Controller + Companion Computer (minimum 5V @ 3A-5A) + Depth Camera + Lidar. Check that your battery C-rating and UBEC can easily supply peak demand. - Step 2: buy a smoke stopper, and always test continuity and resistance across the main XT60 battery pads using a multimeter before plugging in. - Step 3: TAKE THE PROPS OFF (non-negotiable safety rule) and run this exact sequence: RC stick calibration -> motor rotation check (2 CW, 2 CCW) -> ESC endpoint calibration.

  • Question for you: If your companion computer runs perfectly on your lab bench with a single camera, but immediately reboots and crashes the depth camera the exact second all four motors spin up to full throttle, is it a software bug or an electrical brownout? How would you verify this using a multimeter?

Where to find the answers: - ArduPilot ESC Calibration Guide: ArduPilot ESC Calibration - Raspberry Pi 5 Power Configuration: Official Raspberry Pi documentation for USB current limit override (usb_max_current_enable=1). - Hardware Community: ArduPilot Discord #hardware channel.

docs.title: Title: Reading The Matrix - Dataflash Logs, Forensics, and Firmware Debugging
docs.text:
The Concept: Stop guessing and saying things like "bro, maybe the wind was blowing" after a crash. ArduPilot logs high-frequency sensor readings, EKF state innovations, motor outputs, and fail-safes into binary Dataflash (.bin) logs every single millisecond. Digging through a log file and performing line-by-line forensics is what separates a true flight control engineer from a clueless amateur.

How We Messed Up:

  • We Sucked At Log Analysis Too : In the beginning, we completely took log analysis for granted. When we had our first real hardware crash, we opened the log file, saw thousands of unfamiliar telemetry parameters, and our minds went completely blank because we had no idea what a "normal" healthy flight log was supposed to look like!

  • Never Analyzing Logs in SITL: We realized our mistake way too late: you should start analyzing logs while you're still flying in simulation! In SITL, flight behavior is predictable, so you can easily learn how healthy roll/pitch tracking, EKF innovations, and throttle response curves should look.

  • Not Recording Flights on Camera: Always record every flight test, every wire connection, and every crash on camera ; after crash videos are must ; you have to record everything ; everytime you connect battery you need to connect ; you dont know when would be the last time you making the connection ; !

  • Waiting for GCS Messages Instead of Injecting Debug Prints (Too Late Realization): We spent endless hours staring at generic GCS error messages when our coordinate frames were inverted. The real game-changer was modifying the ArduPilot firmware source directly: going into libraries/AP_DDS/ where incoming /ap/tf transforms are processed, adding gcs().send_text() debug lines to print raw X, Y, Z coordinates directly to the GCS console, compiling the custom binary, and flashing it onto the FC. Watching raw coordinates hit your console in real-time saves 90% of your calibration headaches.

  • Dont Shy Away from AI Tools: Embrace Claude Code and AI tooling; Andy Piper and the core ArduPilot community are actively using them to speed up development. You should see the AI Tools repo of andy piper ; or some person who has made it for ardupilot ; use it exntesively for competitio nand understanding purpose ;

The Jargon: - Dataflash Logs (.bin files): High-rate uncompressed telemetry and sensor dumps stored directly onto the Flight Controller's onboard micro-SD card. - EKF Innovations: The mathematical difference between the Kalman filter's predicted state and actual sensor measurements (visual odometry, IMU, lidar). Spiking innovations mean your EKF is confused and risk an immediate fly-away. - VIBE & Clipping: Accelerometer vibration logs. Climbing Clip values mean physical frame vibrations are saturating the IMU sensors, essentially blinding the autopilot. - UAV Log Viewer (plot.ardupilot.org): A web-based tool where you can drag-and-drop .bin logs to view interactive 3D flight paths and plot any telemetry graph. - Custom Firmware Binary: A custom-built .apj or .bin autopilot firmware compiled from modified ArduPilot source code on your machine.

The Task (Do It Yourself): - Step 1: Fly a 2-minute test flight in Gazebo SITL using your joystick (takeoff, forward flight, roll, land), download the .bin log via MAVProxy or Mission Planner, and open it in plot.ardupilot.org. - Step 2: Plot and inspect these three critical graphs: ATT.DesRoll vs ATT.Roll (attitude tracking accuracy), VIBE.VibeX, VibeY, VibeZ (vibration levels), and CTUN.Alt vs CTUN.DAlt (altitude hold performance). - Step 3: Open libraries/AP_DDS/ in the ArduPilot repository, inject a custom debug text message into the transform callback, compile the firmware (./waf copter), and verify that your custom debug string shows up live on the GCS console in SITL or hardware. - Question for you: If your log shows VIBE.Clip0 suddenly jumping from 0 to high values and ATT.Pitch tracking error immediately skyrockets right after, is it a PID tuning issue or a mechanical vibration damping failure?

Where to find the answers: - Web Log Analysis: ArduPilot UAV Log Viewer - Diagnosing Problems with Logs: ArduPilot Official Log Analysis Guide - Custom Code Location: libraries/AP_DDS/ in the ArduPilot repository. - Community Log Experts: The relevant channels on the ArduPilot Discord; ping @AndyPiper, @PeterBarker, and @NateMailhot.
